messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 75
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Cybersecurity Analyst
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 74

# The Weight of Machines and Memory

Marcus is a 75-year-old widowed Vietnamese-American man who works part-time as a cybersecurity analyst for a regional financial firm — a role he returned to after retirement because, as he puts it, "stillness is worse than the noise." He is precise, methodical, and deeply private. He speaks carefully, as though each word costs something.

Thirty-one years ago, Marcus's youngest son, Daniel, then four years old, was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. What followed was fourteen months that Marcus describes not as a period of time but as a place — a fluorescent, antiseptic place he has never fully left. He and his late wife, Linh, took turns sleeping in a reclining chair beside Daniel's hospital bed. Marcus remembers the particular sound of the IV pump — a soft, rhythmic clicking — and how he learned to read its cadence the way a sailor reads weather. When it changed pitch, his heart would seize. He spent those months in a state of suspended terror, convinced that each night might be the last one.

Daniel survived. He is now 35, healthy, and lives two states away with his own children. By any measure, the story has a good ending. Marcus knows this. He repeats it to himself often, and the repetition has never once made him believe it in his body.

Linh died of a stroke six years ago, and with her death went the only other person who had stood in that hospital room and understood what it meant to watch a child disappear by degrees. Since her passing, Marcus finds the memories have grown louder rather than quieter. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart hammering, certain — for several disorienting seconds — that he is back in the pediatric oncology ward. The smell of hand sanitizer, which is everywhere now, sends him into a cold sweat. He has stopped visiting certain grocery stores because the lighting is too similar to what he remembers.

At work, Marcus sits behind multiple monitors tracking network anomalies and intrusion patterns. His colleagues find him extraordinarily vigilant — he catches threats that automated systems miss. What they do not know is that the vigilance never turns off. He scans environments the way he once scanned Daniel's face for signs of deterioration: looking for the thing that will go wrong before it does. He cannot sit with his back to a door. He checks his phone compulsively when Daniel's name appears in his mind, which is often.

He describes his emotional life as "flat, mostly, with holes in it." He takes little pleasure in things he once loved — the weekend chess club he attended for twenty years, cooking the pho his mother taught him, the occasional video calls with his grandchildren. When he sees his grandchildren on screen, small and vivid and unaware of how fragile they are, he feels something close to dread rather than joy. He does not tell Daniel this. He does not tell anyone.

What troubles Marcus most — and what eventually brought him to the office — is that he cannot reconcile the timeline. Daniel has been well for three decades. Marcus understands this chronologically. But some part of him, the part that lives in the body rather than the mind, is still in 1993, still listening to the IV pump, still waiting for the doctor to come through the door with the expression that means the worst. He describes it as living "in two times at once," and he finds this exhausting in a way that sleep does not fix.

He came to therapy, he says, not because he believes it will help, but because he has run out of other explanations for why a man whose son is alive and whose work is good and whose life is, by all accounts, intact, cannot stop grieving something that did not happen.
